week.t: NASA: ESCAPADE’s second spacecraft fires its 9-minute trans-Mars burn over Australia, 6:51 pm Singapore time
NASA: PROMISE, a nuclear-powered Moon rover built from Mars rover spares, to launch in late 2028
Science News: possible red blood cells, chemically confirmed, in a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone
Quanta: the PBR theorem of 2012, now run on an IBM quantum computer, rules out Einstein’s picture of reality
NUS: Prof Mario Lanza’s 2 × 2 µm hexagonal boron nitride radio switches, built into working circuits
ISRO: NVS-03 completes four engine burns, 6,164 seconds in all, and reaches geosynchronous orbit

tiles.cap: Tonight, 6:51 pm here: a Mars probe over Australia fires its engine for 9 minutes and goes
tiles.nums: about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second after the 9-minute burn, which adds more than 1,000 mph
tiles.p1: NASA’s second ESCAPADE spacecraft makes its powered flyby of Earth tonight: its trans-Mars injection burn begins at 5:51 am US Eastern on Monday 9 November, which is 6:51 pm in Singapore, over southern Australia, the burn coming at closest approach, which NASA rounds to around 6 am Eastern, 7 pm here. The first spacecraft was due to do the same on Saturday; NASA’s ESCAPADE blog had not posted its result when this edition was written on Monday morning. A powered flyby, also called an Oberth manoeuvre, combines Earth’s gravity with an engine burn, and NASA says no agency spacecraft had flown one before.
tiles.p2: Why now: Earth and Mars line up for a launch every 26 months. ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when the planets were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the pair loitered around the Earth–Sun Lagrange point 2 and came back to Earth this month to be thrown onward.
deep: How close, how fast

At closest approach the spacecraft pass 600 to 1,100 miles above Earth’s surface, higher than most Earth-orbiting satellites. The burn raises their speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second, Mach 30 to Mach 31; at that speed, NASA says, a craft could fly from Washington, DC, to San Francisco in under 7 minutes.
Then ten months

A 10-month cruise follows. The first spacecraft arrives at Mars on 7 September 2027 and the second on 9 September, the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around Mars, measuring how the solar wind, material from the Sun moving at about a million miles per hour, strips away the Martian atmosphere.
Bonus science

While loitering, the pair passed through a distant part of Earth’s magnetotail that had never been directly explored. NASA says the team saw interesting activity and structure and plans to share findings soon.
Could you see it

Each spacecraft is about the size of a standard refrigerator and faint, so a telescope would most likely be needed. In the days after the burns the team will learn how well each craft is aimed and plan trajectory correction manoeuvres for the Mars rendezvous in September 2027.
tiles.src: NASA ESCAPADE blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, Goddard); blog re-checked Mon 9 Nov, 06:40 SGT
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space/Matt Bolliger, via NASA ESCAPADE blog

tiles.cap: NASA’s next Moon rover: built from Mars rover spares, with a nuclear generator on its back
tiles.nums: how cold the permanently shadowed craters the rover will drive into may get (minus 400 °F)
tiles.p1: On Saturday at the MAX POWER expo at Kennedy Space Center, NASA announced PROMISE, the Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration: an SUV-sized, six-wheeled, nuclear-powered rover for the Moon’s south pole, targeted to launch in late 2028 on an 18-month mission. JPL is building it from a combination of spare flight parts and engineering test models from the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers, including the electronics, body structure and mobility system of the duplicate Curiosity test-bed vehicle. Blue Origin gets a $94 million contract, with an option worth a further $140 million based on performance, to deliver it on its Mark 1 lander.
tiles.p2: Why now: the same announcement gave eight companies places on CLPS 2, a 10-year cargo-lander contract worth up to $10 billion in total, plus about $1.3 billion of launch task orders. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman: “We are building the Moon Base mission by mission.”
deep: A nuclear generator

Power comes from a flight-spare multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator, which NASA describes as essentially a nuclear generator, fitted at the rear of the rover once it reaches the launch site. It lets PROMISE work through the long lunar night and inside permanently shadowed regions, where temperatures may fall to minus 242 °C.
A drill and a dashcam

The TRIDENT drill, from Honeybee Robotics, pulls up soil from as deep as 1 metre in 10-centimetre steps. Spectrometers analyse what comes up; a radiation detector rides along whose earlier version has run for 15 years on Curiosity; and a stereo Lunar Dashcam with its own illuminators is based on Perseverance’s landing cameras.
Shackleton Crater

NASA’s PROMISE page pictures Shackleton Crater, near the Moon’s south pole, about 21 kilometres wide and 4 kilometres deep. Laser altimetry from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has revealed boulders and low hills in its permanently shadowed interior.
For students too

On Sunday NASA opened a $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge in six categories, from power generation and construction to astronaut safety. It is for teams at US high schools and post-secondary schools, with registration by 25 January 2027.
tiles.src: NASA release 26-095, 7 Nov 2026 · NASA PROMISE mission page, updated 7 Nov 2026 · NASA release 26-096, 8 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Four burns, 103 minutes of firing, and India’s navigation satellite is parked 36,000 km up
tiles.nums: total burn time of NVS-03’s liquid apogee motor across four manoeuvres, about 103 minutes
tiles.p1: ISRO reported on 4 November that NVS-03, placed by GSLV-F18 on 30 October at 23:51 IST into an orbit of 170.3 km by 38,080 km, has completed four orbit manoeuvres with a cumulative liquid apogee motor burn of 6,164 seconds. It now sits in a geosynchronous orbit of 35,765 km by 36,196 km, at an inclination ISRO lists as 29.98 degrees, and ISRO says the health of the satellite is normal. The first burn alone, on 31 October at 16:48 IST, lasted 2,174.8 seconds and lifted the low point of the orbit from 170 km to 5,477.6 km.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: NVS-03 is the third satellite of India’s next-generation navigation system, carrying an indigenous atomic clock and adding an L1 signal to the existing L5 and S-band signals, to serve India and a region about 1,500 km around it.
deep: Why four burns

The GSLV left NVS-03 in a long ellipse, 170.3 km at its lowest and 38,080 km at its highest. The liquid apogee motor fired four times, 6,164 seconds in all, turning that ellipse into a near-circle between 35,765 and 36,196 km up.
The clocks on board

NVS-03 carries an indigenous atomic clock alongside procured atomic clocks, and adds an L1 signal to the L5 and S-band signals the series already transmits. ISRO describes it as continuing the navigation services of the IRNSS series.
What it covers
The system’s coverage is the Indian land mass and a region extending about 1,500 km around India’s geopolitical boundary.
The rocket
GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of the GSLV, from the Second Launch Pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, delivering the satellite to a geosynchronous transfer orbit.
tiles.src: ISRO, Final orbit manoeuvring of NVS-03 spacecraft (4 Nov 2026) and Orbit manoeuvring update (31 Oct 2026) · ISRO GSLV-F18 mission page
tiles.credit: Photo: ISRO (GSLV-F18 on the launch pad)

tiles.cap: A 2G system used about 4 radio switches; 6G may need 100. NUS made them 2 micrometres wide
tiles.nums: the size of each hexagonal boron nitride radio-frequency switch, which keeps its state when the power is off
tiles.p1: NUS News profiled Professor Mario Lanza of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering on 6 November. His group’s paper in Nature on 8 July 2026, first author Dr Sebastian Pazos, reported radio-frequency switches made of hexagonal boron nitride, an insulating two-dimensional material, which can be only a single atomic layer thick, each measuring 2 by 2 micrometres. They were integrated onto commercially manufactured gallium nitride microchips and used in working circuits that adjust signal strength, redirect signals and select frequencies. A 2G system used about four such switches; 5G and 6G may need 50 to more than 100.
tiles.p2: Why here: Lanza and Pazos founded the start-up Newmorphic at one-north. On 28 and 29 October it won the Advanced Manufacturing and Industrial Systems domain at SLINGSHOT 2026, a competition that drew more than 5,100 applications from 148 countries.
deep: Resistors with memory
The switches are memristors, which the article describes as resistors with memory: they retain their state after power is removed.
Tunnelling leaks

A second paper, in Nature Materials on 1 July 2026 with Dr Yue Yuan as first author, used conductive atomic force microscopy on 2D materials. Quantum tunnelling, electrons slipping through barriers meant to stop them, increases energy consumption and usually accelerates device failure; the team found that tiny gaps between an atom-thin material and its electrodes change how far electrons travel. Lanza: “tiny physical gaps between electrodes can matter more than the material’s own ability to block electrical current.”
One transistor as a neuron

A 2025 Nature article from the group showed that a single standard silicon transistor can emulate both neural and synaptic behaviour, work that usually takes dozens of transistors and bulky capacitors, pointing at spiking neural networks on battery-powered drones, robots and wearables.
How he works

Lanza says the team repeats experiments multiple times, uses test protocols as close as possible to those industry requires, and reports yield, variability, reliability and stability, with most fabrication on processes compatible with semiconductor wafer lines.
tiles.src: NUS News, “From atoms to systems: Prof Mario Lanza’s push to reinvent the electronics of the future”, 6 Nov 2026 · Nature, 8 Jul 2026 · Nature Materials, 1 Jul 2026

tiles.cap: On the worst hand of a card game, classical physics wins 3 in 4. Quantum wins every time
tiles.nums: a classical player’s odds of being right when the dealer turns up two red aces; a quantum player can always win
tiles.p1: Einstein believed things have definite properties whether or not anyone looks; he once asked a colleague whether he really believed the Moon is not there when nobody is looking at it. He took the quantum wave function to be a summary of our ignorance, like a forecast of 77% rain about a day that will really turn out one way or the other. Quanta Magazine’s Charlie Wood, on 6 November, lays out the two theorems that rule this picture out: Bell’s theorem of 1964, and the PBR theorem of 2012 by Matthew Pusey, Jonathan Barrett and Terry Rudolph, which proved that if the cards have real states, and the first card’s real state does not affect the second’s, the quantum state cannot be mere knowledge.
tiles.p2: Why now: last autumn a Cambridge team led by Crispin Barnes ran a five-card version of the PBR game on an IBM quantum computer. Jacques Pienaar: “From the moment [PBR] came out, people knew it would be a landmark.”
deep: The card game

A dealer draws two cards, each at random from either a pile of 26 red cards or a pile of four aces, and asks the player to name one combination of piles the cards did not come from. Classically, when both cards are red aces the player can be right only 3 times in 4. In the quantum version of the game, the article explains, the player can always win.
Bell first

In 1935 Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen argued quantum theory was incomplete, assuming both reality and locality. John Stewart Bell showed in 1964, inspired by David Bohm’s pilot-wave theory of 1952, that a world both real and local cannot match quantum predictions; experiments in the 1980s sided with quantum mechanics.
Bite or dodge

Pusey: “Do you bite the bullet, or do you try and dodge the bullet?” His view is that if anything is real, the quantum state is real. Pienaar now favours QBism, which holds that the world itself may exist but quantum mechanics cannot describe it.
Watch your sanity

Lucien Hardy of the Perimeter Institute: “You have to watch out for your sanity in a field like quantum foundations.” David Schmid, also at Perimeter, wants a notion of reality that rings true enough that “when people see it, they can’t unsee it”.
tiles.src: Quanta Magazine, “A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality”, Charlie Wood, 6 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A speaker that plays 40 hours, and when the battery finally wears out you swap it yourself
tiles.nums: playtime claimed by Marshall; 20 minutes on a 30 W USB-C charger gives 7 hours
tiles.p1: Marshall’s Stockwell III, on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list, is a 1.3 kg portable speaker shaped like a mini version of the brand’s amps. Marshall’s specification page lists more than 40 hours of playtime, a full charge in under 3 hours on a 30 W USB-C cable, and a lithium-ion battery that is both rechargeable and replaceable; TIME calls a replaceable battery “essentially unheard of in consumer electronics”. Inside are one 3-inch woofer and two 1.75-inch full-range drivers in a sealed enclosure with a passive radiator, covering 54 to 20,000 Hz, with a maximum of 86 dB at 1 metre.
tiles.p2: The engineering choices: Bluetooth 5.3 with Auracast and the LC3 codec, a 10 m range, an IP55 rating, 27% recycled material by product, and firmware updates promised for at least two years after the last unit is sold.
deep: What reviewers found wrong

TechRadar’s Harry Padoan (18 August 2026): “At $249.99 / £199.99 / AU$379, the Stockwell III isn’t the cheapest option on the market”; the sound “does have a bit of a bass preference”; it is “only IP55”; “there’s no LDAC for higher-res Bluetooth playback”; and it still used “the older Marshall Bluetooth app”. Tom’s Guide’s Nikita Achanta: “Given its hefty weight, the Stockwell III isn’t the most portable speaker around.”
What they liked

Padoan called it “a spectacular Bluetooth speaker that offers a substantial upgrade on its predecessor”, with “regimented, intent-filled bass”. Achanta found that “all the buttons and dials give great tactile feedback” and that the treble “felt vibrant and nuanced without becoming fatiguing”.
A number to watch

Marshall notes that some of its packaging may still say “35+ hours”; the figure rose to 40+ after final validation. Tom’s Guide’s Achanta played it at 50% volume and found it ran “just over 40 hours, keeping in line with Marshall’s claims”.
Designed where
Marshall lists the speaker as developed and designed in Sweden and manufactured in Thailand, 180 × 162 × 74 mm, with a strap and a USB-C cable in the box.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Eliza Thompson, 15 Oct 2026) · Marshall Stockwell III specifications · TechRadar review (Harry Padoan, 18 Aug 2026) · Tom’s Guide review (Nikita Achanta, 18 Aug 2026)

tiles.cap: Inside a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone: possible red blood cells. Not everyone agrees
tiles.nums: the size of the ellipsoid structures found inside the bone’s fossilised blood-vessel canals
tiles.p1: A limb bone of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a small feathered theropod that lived about 115 million years ago in what is now northeastern Brazil, holds ellipsoid microstructures about 20 micrometres across inside its fossilised network of blood vessels. In PNAS on 2 November, Kliti Grice of Curtin University and colleagues report iron, carbon and nitrogen, the components of heme, in the structures, a laser light-scattering signal pointing to porphyrins, and a bone-extract analysis that ruled out chlorophyll contamination. They call them the oldest red blood cell structures identified and the first chemically proven.
tiles.p2: The time capsule: hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral inside the structures, may have protected cells and molecules, including collagen amino acids, rather than simply replacing biological material after it disappeared.
deep: Not convinced

Mary Schweitzer of North Carolina State University, who in 2005 reported soft, flexible blood-vessel tissue from a 68-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus rex leg bone: “I am not convinced.” She notes that the heme signals come from the whole bone, not only the round structures, and that the proposed cells differ in size and shape from those of living birds and reptiles.
Convergence

Grice’s reply is that the case “rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry”, and that this kind of preservation “may not be quite as rare as we currently think”. She accepts that no one knows the original shape of dinosaur red blood cells or how fossilisation distorts them.
Fooled before

In 1997 spheres in a possible pterosaur fossil, once thought to be blood cells, turned out to be pyrite. Schweitzer: “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”
Where
The bone came from the Mina Pedra Branca site in northeastern Brazil, and the dinosaur is a Cretaceous species. The picture in the pop-out is an artist’s rendition of Aratasaurus.
tiles.src: Science News, “This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize”, Carolyn Gramling, 6 Nov 2026 · PNAS, 2 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Image: Maurilio Oliveira / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0), via Science News

tiles.cap: Gravity’s constant is the one physicists cannot pin down. 225 years on, labs disagree
tiles.nums: the size of the disagreements between recent measurements of big G, while other constants are known to six or more digits
tiles.p1: NIST announced on 16 April 2026 a new value for the gravitational constant, big G: 6.67387 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻², the end of a 10-year experiment plus two more years of analysis. Scientists have been measuring G for over 225 years, since Henry Cavendish in 1798 hung two lead balls on a horizontally suspended wooden beam with two heavier masses nearby, yet recent measurements disagree with one another by about one part in 10,000, while other constants are known to six or more significant digits. NIST’s value is 0.0235% lower than the French result it set out to replicate.
tiles.p2: The weakest force: gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces. A pin-head magnet lifts a paper clip against the pull of the whole Earth, which is what makes G so hard to measure with laboratory masses about 500 billion trillion times smaller than the planet.
deep: Hair-thin ribbon

Eight cylindrical metal masses: four on a rotating carousel, like four candlesticks in an old-fashioned chandelier, and four smaller ones inside on a disk hung from a copper-beryllium ribbon about the thickness of a human hair. The apparatus replicates an experiment run in 2007 at the BIPM in Sèvres, France.
An envelope

To stop himself unconsciously steering the result toward the expected value, NIST physicist Stephan Schlamminger had colleague Patrick Abbott subtract a secret number from the weights of some masses and put it in an envelope. The true result was revealed at 3 pm on 11 July 2024 at a meeting in Aurora, Colorado; an earlier reveal in 2022 was aborted at the last minute.
Little g and big G

Newton’s law is F = G m₁m₂/r². Little g, the acceleration you feel, is about 9.8 m/s² at Earth’s surface and 1.62 m/s² on the Moon; big G is the universal constant in the formula, and Cavendish measured it a century after Newton published the law.
Why bother
Schlamminger: “Every measurement is important, because the truth matters.” He says he will leave the remaining puzzle to younger generations of scientists.
tiles.src: NIST News, “NIST Weighs In on the Mystery of the Gravitational Constant”, 16 Apr 2026 (updated 5 May 2026) · Metrologia, 16 Apr 2026

tiles.cap: NASA is hiring astronauts. Last time, more than 8,000 people applied and 10 got in
tiles.nums: applicants were chosen for NASA’s 2025 astronaut class; applications for the next class opened on Saturday
tiles.p1: NASA opened applications on Saturday 7 November for its next class of astronauts, who it says will join the agency as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. US citizens have until 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December to submit their applications, and NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027. The agency last opened applications in 2024: from more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are now completing nearly two years of training.
tiles.p2: Why now: applications opened on Saturday 7 November and close at 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December; final selection is expected in late 2027, when training begins.
deep: The numbers
Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates. The agency has 32 astronauts active in its astronaut corps today.
If you want to fly it

For pilots, NASA lists 750 hours as pilot in command of high-performance jet aircraft, or 1,500 total flight hours in other fixed-wing aircraft including 750 as pilot in command, or 1,000 total flight hours in rotary-wing aircraft including 300 as pilot in command. Only US citizens can apply.
What they said

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, adding that the missions “will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage.” Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson put it shorter: “The window is open. The mission is waiting.”
Who picks

Scott Tingle, chief astronaut, chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston; for those who apply, he says, becoming a NASA astronaut “is more than a career opportunity”. The photo shows NASA announcing its 2025 astronaut candidate class at Johnson on 22 September 2025.
tiles.src: NASA news release 26-093, 7 Nov 2026 · NASA media advisory M26-084 (MAX POWER key events), updated 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: “If you are interested in human-level AI, don’t work on LLMs.” LeCun at NTU, plus pushback
tiles.p1: On 3 November Yann LeCun, Jacob T. Schwartz Professor at NYU and executive chairman of Advanced Machine Intelligence, gave the Lee Kong Chian Distinguished Professor public lecture at NTU’s College of Computing and Data Science, titled “World Models: Enabling the Next AI Revolution”. His argument: large language models struggle to reach human-like intelligence, and the better route is world models, systems that build a model of an environment, learn its rules and predict outcomes from their own inputs rather than mainly from human writing. His closing slide urged AI scientists to set aside generative models, probabilistic models, contrastive methods and reinforcement learning.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: NTU’s own write-up, published 6 November, carries the responses of three of its professors rather than only the famous visitor’s view.
deep: Agree

Nanyang Assistant Professor Zhang Mengmi, who works on AI and computational neuroscience: “I strongly agree with Yann LeCun that language cannot be the foundation of human-like intelligence.” She argued that agents should actively seek information and learn from experience, and, taking up LeCun’s description of reinforcement learning as the “cherry on the cake”, said “someone has to figure out how to make the cherry!”.
Disagree

Associate Professor Stefano V. Albrecht, who leads the Autonomous Agents Research Group: “Reinforcement learning is one of the most fundamental principles of learning in natural and artificial systems.” World models, he said, do not remove the difficulty of making decisions under uncertainty.
Half and half

Professor Jordan Boyd-Graber acknowledged a “long history of Yann being right when I was wrong” and agreed that scaling and tweaking LLMs is a scientific dead end, but said “I think the evidence shows that AI progress is grounded in language”, since so much of humanity’s knowledge is stored in writing.
Advice to students

In a fireside chat hosted by Professor Bo An, LeCun advised students to take up physics and engineering, and said: “Basic programming is dead. But computer science is more alive than ever and more important than ever.”
tiles.src: NTU College of Computing and Data Science news, “Are World Models the Future of AI?”, 6 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Mars and Jupiter pass 1.2° apart on 15–16 November, and three supermoons start on the 24th
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors at best, before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set
tiles.p1: NASA’s What’s Up for November 2026, presented by Raquel Villanueva of JPL: the Southern Taurids peaked around 5 November with occasional bright fireballs; the Northern Taurids follow around the 12th at about five meteors an hour under ideal conditions; Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish; and the Leonids are best before dawn on 17–18 November, up to around 15 an hour under ideal skies.
tiles.p2: Why now: the Southern Taurids peaked around 5 November, the Northern Taurids follow around the 12th, and the full Moon on 24 November is the first of three supermoons in a row.
deep: Moon phases
NASA lists November’s Moon phases in US Pacific Time: third quarter on the 1st, new Moon on the 8th, first quarter on the 17th, full supermoon on the 24th, third quarter again on the 30th.
1.2 degrees
Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter and Mars reddish. NASA says both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye.
A light-day away
This month Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a signal travelling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach it. NASA celebrates on 17 November.
Seeing meteors
NASA’s advice for the Leonids: find a dark location and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust. The hours to try are before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Glasses with a 70° view, 1920×1200 per eye, 95 g. The computer lives in your pocket
tiles.nums: for the glasses; the tethered puck that does the computing weighs 265 g and carries a 4,455 mAh battery
tiles.p1: XREAL’s Aura, on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list, puts the computing power in a tethered puck that clips over a pocket or hangs on a lanyard, so the glasses themselves weigh 95 g. Each eye gets a Sony micro-OLED at 1920 × 1200 pixels, up to 120 Hz, with a 70-degree field of view through XREAL’s X Prism optics and electrochromic dimming in five steps. Three cameras sit on the front frame: two tracking cameras for hand tracking and spatial anchoring, and one RGB camera with a privacy LED.
tiles.p2: Why now: XREAL says shipping is expected to begin in mid-November 2026, at US$1,099 on its US store, with the US, Canada, Japan and South Korea first.
deep: The puck

It runs Android XR on a Snapdragon platform rated at 48 TOPS of AI processing, with 12 or 16 GB of memory, a fan for cooling and a 4,455 mAh rated battery. It takes Bluetooth keyboards, mice and game controllers, and has a fingerprint button.
Latency
XREAL’s X1S co-processor in the glasses is rated at 3 ms motion-to-photon latency. Brightness is rated up to 1,050 nits.
What reviewers found wrong

Tom’s Guide’s Jason England, trying them at Google I/O in May, saw “some edge blurring”, found it “slower to do things than on an actual computer”, and wrote that “you won’t be taking these outside in public without getting second looks”. He estimated the puck is “probably good for 2-3 hours of heavy use”; XREAL lists no battery life in hours.
The price problem

England: “while I’d love for these to be sub-$1,000, I don’t see a world where this happens.” TechRadar’s Hamish Hector, trying them at IFA in September, hoped for the same and noted “there’s only so cheap we can expect XR tech to get”.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Richard Eisenberg, 15 Oct 2026) · XREAL Aura specifications and US store · Tom’s Guide hands-on (Jason England, updated 21 May 2026) · TechRadar (Hamish Hector, 4 Sep 2026)

tiles.cap: Eyes shut, hands up: touch your nose, then your left thumb. Now wiggle the fingers, retry
tiles.p1: Close your eyes and raise both hands above your head, keeping the fingers of your left hand completely still. With your right hand, quickly touch your right index fingertip to your nose, then to the tip of your left thumb. Go back to your nose and try each left fingertip in turn, then switch hands. The Exploratorium’s Proprioception snack asks: how accurately did you find each fingertip, did you improve, and did left and right differ? Now repeat with the fingers of the raised hand wiggling.
tiles.p2: Why wiggling helps: moving fingers feed the brain extra information about where they are, so they become easier to locate in space; repetition improves the result too.
deep: The sixth sense

Proprioceptors, also called stretch receptors, in your muscles, tendons, joints and inner ear send position information to the brain, which works out how your body is oriented and moving. Most people lean heavily on vision for position and distance, so proprioception alone gives imprecise results.
Who used it

The Exploratorium pairs the snack with Dr Patricia Cowings, a psychophysiologist who trained as a NASA astronaut, was an alternate for a 1979 spaceflight, developed individually tailored protocols to prevent motion sickness in astronauts, and is principal investigator at NASA Ames Research Center.
Two more versions
The same page has two further activities, marking an X and writing with eyes shut, which need paper and pencil. The hands-only version needs nothing at all.

tiles.cap: A river that travels 5.5 miles to get 1.3 miles, photographed from the space station
tiles.nums: miles the San Juan River flows (8.9 km) between two points only 1.3 miles (2.1 km) apart
tiles.p1: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed this stretch of the San Juan River in southern Utah on 6 October 2026. The river flows through a series of entrenched meanders, also known as goosenecks, on its westward path to Lake Powell. In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park it runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 metres) deep, and one section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 km) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 km) apart.
tiles.p2: Why now: it was NASA Earth Observatory’s Image of the Day for 6 November 2026.
deep: How a river got stuck in rock

Tens of millions of years ago, NASA says, the San Juan shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River. Some experts think that, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s rise elevated the river’s headwaters, which increased its gradient and sped its flow. The river cut through 300-million-year-old rock.
The camera

This is astronaut photograph ISS075-E-188830, taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimetres. NASA says the image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed.
Dark skies

The park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. NASA notes that in November 2026 the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids and Leonids reach their peaks.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Image of the Day for 6 Nov 2026 (story by Lindsey Doermann)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA / ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Johnson Space Center

tiles.cap: Two people, one screen, different colours. Sometimes the display is at fault
tiles.nums: types of cone cell in the eye; displays mix red, green and blue to target them, but not everyone’s cones respond the same way
tiles.p1: People perceive colours differently, especially on modern displays that produce a wide range of colours, reports Physics World. Colour vision works thanks to three types of cone photoreceptor cells, and almost all display technologies exploit this by using red, green and blue. The problem with newer displays, Physics World explains, is that they do not necessarily activate the cones of different observers equally. The work was led by Andy Rider of the Institute of Ophthalmology at University College London.
tiles.p2: How it started: Rider says the work began when display technology consultant John Frith got in touch with his group, after a friend of Frith’s in the film industry saw the colours of two side-by-side cinema projectors as wildly different.
deep: Where it is published
The research was led by Andy Rider of UCL’s Institute of Ophthalmology and is published in Optics Express (DOI 10.1364/OE.613255).
The friend’s eyes

The Physics World anecdote has a twist: when Rider’s group tested the friend who saw the two projectors so differently, he turned out to have a red–green colour-vision deficiency he had not known about. Rider says he has the same condition and was not properly diagnosed until his mid-30s. Displays can drive cones unequally, and eyes differ too.
Three cones

The three cone types are called L, M and S, and each one responds to different wavelengths of visible light. When two people’s cones differ, the same red, green and blue mix on a display can look different to each of them, what Physics World calls colour mismatches, or metamerism failures.
tiles.src: Physics World, “Why do people see colours differently? Sometimes, it’s the display’s fault”, Isabelle Dumé, 5 Nov 2026 · Optics Express

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, doing 48% better on the problems. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: the researchers say the students used the bot as a “crutch” and did not learn the underlying concepts deeply enough.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, different result.
What the researchers concluded

The worry is that students use a plain chatbot as a crutch. The hint-only tutor, designed to guide students instead of directly giving answers, avoided the damage. The researchers call the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later.
